children: By Sharon Kimathi

Today’s newsletter focuses on climate financing discussions at the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York this week, as the event coincided with the New York Climate Week in the run-up to the Conference of the Parties (COP31) in November.
This year’s COP31 summit will be held in the southern Turkish province of Antalya from November 9 to 20.
Under an arrangement, Australia will ​lead formal negotiations at COP31, with Turkey responsible for the presidency and ​action agenda.

Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan said at the UN General Assembly that it was unrealistic to expect all countries to make the same progress on climate policy ​while inequalities in access to financing and technology persisted, adding ‌he expected support from all nations for Turkey's COP31 Climate Summit action agenda.

"Steps that will ​strengthen countries' prosperity must be shaped by their own ​conditions, ⁠resources and development priorities. While inequalities persist over access to financing and technology, it is not realistic to expect all countries to advance at ⁠the ​same pace," he added.

Sticking with the theme of inequality in climate financing, Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah called for grant-based international support at the UN General Assembly to help the ​Himalayan nation recover from the glacier flood that killed ‌at least 1,450 people.

The Nepalese leader said the flood, which he described as a warning of the growing risks posed by climate change, had swept away roads, bridges, schools, homes and livelihoods, interrupting Nepal's development progress.
Shah said Nepal's recovery and reconstruction needs were estimated at about 10% of gross domestic product following the ​flood that struck mountain communities four weeks ago.
He argued ​that vulnerable countries should not be forced to take ⁠on additional debt to rebuild from catastrophic climate events.

"When a climate-driven disaster ​destroys infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be ​another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants," Shah said. "We need adequate grant-based support from the world."
Other climate financing pledges were announced by Britain, the European Union and Canada this week.

Britain said it would provide £331 million ($438 million) to ​help tackle climate change and biodiversity loss-driven instability, while the European Commission and Canada secured at least €211 million ($240 million) in funding pledges ​for a newly launched ocean observation initiative.
CLIMATE BUZZ
Heavy rains hit Mexico as Hurricane Polo tracks offshore

Hurricane Polo lashed southwestern Mexico with heavy surf and rain as it moved slowly northwest off the Pacific coast, the US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said. As the NHC keeps adjusting the storm's force, it said it could see ​some near-term strengthening and is expected to remain a major hurricane for the next few days.
Countries still way behind on UN biodiversity targets

Governments are on track to miss a key goal of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the landmark UN agreement struck in 2022 to protect at least 30% of the world's land and oceans by 2030, according to research from environmental groups led by Campaign for Nature and Together for the Ocean.
Trump rolled back regulations for oil company campaign donors, Democrats say

Senators Chuck Schumer, ​the Democratic leader, and Sheldon Whitehouse, the top Democrat on the environment committee, launched a report in the US Senate that showed oil and gas companies were rewarded with tax breaks, subsidies and rollbacks of environmental regulation after then-candidate Donald ​Trump asked them for $1 billion in donations during the 2024 presidential campaign. Click here to read more about the findings of their investigation.
Top dairy exporter Fonterra flags El Niño risks to milk supply

New Zealand's ‌Fonterra warned that El Niño could affect milk volume growth at the end of the 2026/27 season, as the weather phenomenon heightens risk of extreme weather events and impacts global crop output. Click here for an in-depth explainer on the super El Niño weather phenomenon and click here for more on Fonterra’s reduced milk production warning.
Minerals and pandas: US-China talks and what it means for environmental and governance issues

US President Donald Trump met with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping for diplomatic and trade discussions. Among the environmental and governance themes hanging over the talks was China's dominance in rare earths. Despite a surge in US production, the US is expected to remain dependent on Chinese supplies well into the 2030s. Click here to find out why.
Xi also revived China's long-running "panda diplomacy", announcing that two giant pandas will soon arrive at Zoo Atlanta. Click here to read more about Ping Ping and Fu Shuang.
